name: Anduril

Software Engineer.dsaDepth: Heavy - deliberately ambiguous, multi-phase coding prompts where extracting requirements IS part of the evaluation, plus genuine mission-alignment screening throughout, and a hard eligibility gate before any of it
rounds: Eligibility gate (before anything else): most roles require US person status under ITAR export-control regulations, and many require security-clearance eligibility - confirm this before investing time
Recruiter phone screen (30-60 min): technical background AND genuine motivation for working in the defense sector - evaluated here and re-checked in every later round, not just once

Technical phone screen (~60 min, HackerRand-style live coding): often an intentionally vague, multi-phase prompt (e.g. a circular-queue reader/writer to debug, or a Queue problem building on itself) - asking clarifying questions before coding is part of what’s being tested

Final round (4 back-to-back ~60 min sessions, same day): 2 coding rounds (graphs are the most commonly reported topic - BFS and traversal variants), 1 OOD/system-design round (real-time, failure-tolerant systems, sometimes tailored to Anduril’s defense domain), 1 behavioral conversation with a senior staff member
C++ memory-management and multithreading/concurrency questions reported for some systems-focused roles
extraTopics: Extracting requirements from a deliberately incomplete prompt BEFORE committing to a design - candidates who charge straight into code against imagined requirements are reported to fail a test they didn’t know was running
Sustained, genuine enthusiasm for defense-sector work, checked by multiple people across the process, not a single "why us" question
C++ memory/concurrency fundamentals for systems roles (circular buffers, reader/writer patterns)
Software Engineer.notes: Process moves fast (3-4 weeks typical, next-day feedback between rounds reported), though some candidates describe it as occasionally rushed or disorganized.
